content.value_statement: Swift concurrency errors can hide data-race and isolation problems that are difficult to diagnose. This skill provides structured, safety-focused guidance for async/await, actors, Sendable, and Swift 6 migration.
actual_capabilities: Diagnose common Swift concurrency compiler and SwiftLint warnings.
Identify actor and main-actor isolation boundaries before proposing changes.
Refactor callback-based asynchronous code toward async/await patterns.
Recommend structured concurrency tools for sequential and parallel work.
Guide incremental Swift 6 migration with build and test validation.
Explain Sendable, task cancellation, Core Data, and concurrency testing concerns.
limitations: It cannot inspect project settings or source files unless you provide access.
It cannot prove runtime data-race safety without builds, tests, and profiling.
It does not replace code review for unsafe annotations or public API changes.
Guidance may need adjustment for your Swift, Xcode, and dependency versions.

use_cases.title: Resolve a compiler diagnostic
use_cases.description: Trace a Swift concurrency warning to its isolation boundary and choose the smallest safe fix.

use_cases.title: Plan a Swift 6 migration
use_cases.description: Break a migration into verified, reviewable changes for Sendable and actor-isolation diagnostics.

use_cases.title: Review async architecture
use_cases.description: Choose actors, task groups, and cancellation handling for a new concurrent feature.

prompt_templates.title: Explain one warning
prompt_templates.prompt: Explain this Swift concurrency compiler warning and show the smallest safe fix: [paste diagnostic and code].

prompt_templates.title: Fix actor isolation
prompt_templates.prompt: Review this type for actor-isolation mistakes. State the intended ownership boundary, then propose a minimal change: [paste code].

prompt_templates.title: Convert callbacks
prompt_templates.prompt: Convert this callback-based API to async/await. Preserve error handling, cancellation behavior, and the public API where possible: [paste code].

prompt_templates.title: Plan a migration
prompt_templates.prompt: Create an incremental Swift 6 concurrency migration plan for this module. Ask for unknown build settings, group diagnostics, and include build and test checks: [details].

output_examples.input: A MainActor-isolated property is accessed from a background task.
output: Recommends a narrow main-actor hop only for the UI update.
Lists a build and actor-sensitive test check.

output_examples.input: A callback API must be migrated to async/await.
output: Maps success and failure callbacks to a throwing async function.
Explains continuation safety and cancellation considerations.
Suggests tests for success, failure, and cancellation.

best_practices: Provide the exact diagnostic, relevant code, and Swift or Xcode version.
Confirm build settings and default isolation before making migration-sensitive changes.
Build and test each small concurrency change before continuing.
anti_patterns: Do not add @MainActor as a blanket response to every warning.
Do not use @unchecked Sendable without a documented thread-safety invariant.
Do not batch unrelated concurrency fixes into one unverified change.

faq.question: Does this skill support Swift 6?
faq.answer: Yes. It provides guidance for strict concurrency checking, Sendable requirements, and isolation diagnostics.

faq.question: Can it fix data races automatically?
faq.answer: No. It can propose changes, but you must build, test, and review the result in your project.

faq.question: Should I share project settings?
faq.answer: Yes. Language mode, strict concurrency, and default isolation affect correct advice.

faq.question: Can it convert callback APIs?
faq.answer: Yes. It can outline async/await conversions while preserving error and cancellation behavior.

faq.question: When should I use an actor?
faq.answer: Use an actor for shared mutable state when serialized ownership expresses the design clearly.

faq.question: Does it replace Instruments or tests?
faq.answer: No. Use tests and Instruments to validate behavior, cancellation, memory, and performance claims.
